checkpoints: A monitoring backend stores one time series per unique combination of label values on a metric, not a single running count per metric name — so the number of stored series scales with the label key space, not with "how many requests happened."

Labels whose values only ever come from a small fixed set — an HTTP method, a route template, a status code — keep a counter's series count bounded no matter how much traffic arrives, because the same combinations just get incremented again.

A label whose value is unique per event — a freshly generated request UUID, or a per-user id — mints a brand-new time series on every single occurrence, so the series count grows without bound as traffic grows, eventually causing monitoring-backend RAM pressure, slow queries, scrape timeouts, and OOM.

Using the raw request path (e.g. `/users/123`) as a label instead of the route template (e.g. `/users/:id`) has the same unbounded effect as a user or request id, since every distinct resource id in the URL becomes its own series.

The fix is to shrink the counter's label set to only bounded values — method, a templated route, and status code — and drop the per-user and per-request labels from the metric entirely, using something like the middleware's own route-resolution helper to collapse concrete URLs into their template.

Removing an identity label from a metric does not sacrifice per-request debuggability: user id, request id, and trace id still belong in structured logs and distributed traces, which are built for high-cardinality, per-event detail in a way metrics are not — the two data types are meant to be tied together via a shared identifier like `trace_id` rather than merged into one.

The trade-off of this fix is honest, not free: you lose the ability to filter this exact user or request straight out of the metric itself, in exchange for the same forensic detail via a logs/traces lookup — a fair trade since metrics were never designed for per-event forensics.

The change can be verified by checking the monitoring backend's head series count (e.g. Prometheus's `numSeries`) before and after — confirming it stops climbing — and by checking that query p95/p99 latency and scrape duration return to normal budgets.
